title: Paying for Televisions That Did Not Exist: Legend's First Deal
dek: The Beijing researchers who started the company later called Lenovo lost most of their 200,000 yuan on a television deal, then went back to the computers they knew.

story.event: Losing most of the start-up money on colour televisions that never existed, then turning to computer work
story.summary: In late 1984 eleven researchers from the Chinese Academy of Sciences, Liu Chuanzhi among them, started a company in Beijing with 200,000 yuan from the Academy. Their first big deal, buying colour televisions to resell, was a con that cost about two-thirds of the money. They recovered by servicing and checking computers and selling a Chinese-character card; the company later became Lenovo and in 2004 agreed to buy IBM's PC business.
paragraphs: On 17 October 1984, eleven researchers from the Chinese Academy of Sciences' computing institute in Beijing met to discuss starting a company. One of them was Liu Chuanzhi, then forty; another, Wang Shuhe, became its first general manager. According to Ling Zhijun's history of the firm, they had no business plan, two small rooms in a former guard post lately used as a bicycle shed, and 200,000 yuan from the Academy, a loan arranged by Liu's superior. Liu later said the sum would not have bought three computers in China at the time.

To raise working money, they decided to buy colour televisions wholesale and sell them at retail. Ling records that the trade was full of confidence tricks, and the new company paid 140,000 yuan for televisions that did not exist. Speaking in Hangzhou in 2009, Liu said the company had been scammed out of two-thirds of its money. "When we came out, we not only lacked funds but also had no idea what to do," he said. An attempt to sell an electronic watch failed as well. In 1997 he told Asiaweek, "We were mainly scientists and didn't understand the market."

What they did have was what they knew. The institute let the company sell some of its research, and the chief engineer, Ni Guangnan, brought in a card that let personal computers handle Chinese characters. The company took on servicing and training for 500 computers the institute had bought, and did work for IBM's agency in Beijing. Mure Dickie of the Financial Times later wrote that the group rebuilt its hopes mainly through a year of hard work checking PCs for new buyers. Liu remembered his first meeting of IBM agents, in 1985, when he sat in the back row.

The character card became the company's breakthrough product, and in 1990 Legend made its first PC under its own brand. Renamed Lenovo in 2003, it agreed in late 2004 to buy IBM's personal computer business for $1.75 billion. "Even in my dreams, I never imagined that one day we could buy the IBM PC business," Liu said.

quote.text: To know and yet (think) we do not know is the highest (attainment); not to know (and yet think) we do know is a disease.
quote.source_title: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics, tr. James Legge, Project Gutenberg eBook #216
quote.connection: Laozi counts it a sickness to think you know what you do not. The television deal was a trip into a trade the founders did not understand; Liu's later plain admission that they had no idea what to do is the start of the cure the line describes.

reflection: Liu never pretended the television deal was clever. Years later he said plainly that they were scientists who did not understand the market, and that admission is the useful part of the story. The con did not teach them a better trading trick. It sent them back to the work they understood: checking machines, training users, making computers read Chinese.

You will be offered side routes as well: a quick piece of work outside your field, a deal that would pay for the next few months. Some will be sound. Laozi's question is not whether to try them, but whether you can say honestly which part you do not understand, and who does.
invitation: Take one decision in front of you this week and write down the single part of it you understand least. Then name one person who knows that part better, and ask them one question about it.

cross_checks.claim: Eleven researchers started the company in 1984 with 200,000 yuan from the Chinese Academy of Sciences.
The first big deal, buying colour televisions, failed.
The company was cheated out of most of its capital: about two-thirds (Liu) or 140,000 of 200,000 yuan (Ling Zhijun).
Recovery came through computer work: quality checks and servicing, and a Chinese-character card that became the breakthrough product.
Lenovo agreed in late 2004 to buy IBM's PC business for $1.75 billion.

research_notes: Amount lost: Liu himself, as reported by PCWorld (2009), said the company was scammed out of two-thirds of its 200,000 yuan; Ling Zhijun's company history (as summarised by Summaries.com) gives RMB 140,000 paid for colour TVs that did not exist. These are consistent (two-thirds is about 133,000), so the story gives both, each attributed. Neither English source says who arranged the TV deal or names the swindler, so the story says 'the new company' and does not put the loss on Liu personally. Date: the company was founded in late 1984 (Ling dates the founders' meeting to 17 October; Wikipedia gives incorporation on 1 November); the English sources call the TV deal the company's first big deal but do not date it, so the slate's '1985' is not stated and approx_date is 1984. Founder role: Ling names Wang Shuhe as the first general manager; Liu is widely described as the founder and later led the company, so the story names Wang briefly. Capital in dollars varies by source ($24,000 Gale; $25,000 FT; $28,600 Caixin; $30,000 'today' PCWorld; $40,000 Summaries.com), so the story gives only yuan. The room: Ling (via the summary) about twenty square metres; Gale 'barely 20 square yards'; Caixin 20 square metres; the story does not give a size. Ling's book itself was not available; the Summaries.com PDF summary is cited for it and its compressed text is not always readable by name checks, so every claim it supports is also backed by PCWorld, the FT piece or the Gale company history except the 140,000 figure, the guard post and Wang Shuhe, which are attributed to Ling. The Summaries.com figures for first-year revenue (RMB 3.5 million) were left out because no second source gives them. The Mure Dickie article appeared in the Financial Times in December 2004 and was republished by Chief Executive in 2005. The Asiaweek quotation (13 June 1997) is taken from the Gale biography. Industry set to computers (the slate said software).
